Limiting sum $= 2^0 + 2^{-1} + 2^{-2} + \cdots$

parts.latex: Which of the following is the value of $\int_0^{10} f(x)\,dx$ ?

solutions.latex:
Split the area into pieces, using the grid:

From $x=0$ to $x=2$ the area is a trapezium with parallel sides $2$ and $1$ and height $2$: $\dfrac{1}{2}\times 2\times(2+1)=3$.

From $x=2$ to $x=6$ the area is a rectangle $4\times 2=8$ with a semicircle of radius $2$ on top: $\dfrac{1}{2}\times\pi\times 2^2=2\pi$.

From $x=6$ to $x=8$ the quarter circle of radius $2$ is above the axis (area $\pi$), and from $x=8$ to $x=10$ the quarter circle of radius $2$ is below the axis (area $-\pi$), so they cancel.
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^{10}f(x)\,dx&=3+(8+2\pi)+(\pi-\pi) \\ &=11+2\pi\end{aligned}$$

\exfigure{1614_q18_1}

Upper and lower rectangles of width $0.5$ units are drawn from the $x$-axis to the curve between $x=1$ and $x=2$ as shown in the diagram.

By considering the areas of the rectangles, show that $\dfrac{7}{24}<\ln\sqrt{2}<\dfrac{5}{12}$.

solutions.latex:
The curve $y=\dfrac{1}{2x}$ is decreasing, so the lower rectangles have area less than the integral and the upper rectangles have area greater than it.

The heights are $y=\dfrac{1}{2}$ at $x=1$, $y=\dfrac{1}{3}$ at $x=1.5$ and $y=\dfrac{1}{4}$ at $x=2$.

Lower rectangles:
$$\dfrac{1}{3}\times\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{4}\times\dfrac{1}{2}=\dfrac{7}{24}$$
Upper rectangles:
$$\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{3}\times\dfrac{1}{2}=\dfrac{5}{12}$$
The exact area is
$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^2\dfrac{dx}{2x} &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\ln x\right]_1^2 \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}(\ln2-\ln1) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\ln2 \\ &= \ln\sqrt2 \end{aligned}$$
Hence
$$\dfrac{7}{24}<\ln\sqrt2<\dfrac{5}{12}$$
criteria: Both rectangle sums correct and integral evaluated to $\ln\sqrt2$, or equivalent merit
Both rectangle sums correct, or equivalent merit

figures.cap: graph of y=f(x): rectangle, quarter-circle sector and triangle

solutions.latex:
The integral is the signed area between the graph and the $x$-axis, found piece by piece.

For $-3\le x\le 0$ the rectangle has width $3$ and height $2$, above the axis.
$$A_1 = 3\times 2 = 6$$
For $0\le x\le 2$ the sector is a quarter of a circle of radius $2$, above the axis.
$$A_2 = \dfrac{1}{4}\pi (2)^2 = \pi$$
For $2\le x\le 5$ the triangle has base $3$ and height $1$, below the axis, so its area counts as negative.
$$A_3 = -\dfrac{1}{2}\times 3\times 1 = -\dfrac{3}{2}$$
Adding the three areas,
$$\begin{aligned} \int_{-3}^{5} f(x)\,dx &= 6+\pi-\dfrac{3}{2} \\ &= \pi+\dfrac{9}{2} \end{aligned}$$
This is option A.

parts.latex:

\exfigure{1344_q8_1}

Find the value of $P$, given:

$$\int_{-P}^{P}(P-|x|)\,dx=16$$
can_use: Integrals of odd and even functions

solutions.latex:
The graph of $y=P-|x|$ is a triangle above the $x$-axis between $x=-P$ and $x=P$, with apex $(0,P)$. The $y$-intercept is positive, so $P>0$. This rules out options C and D.

The integral is the area of this triangle, with base $2P$ and height $P$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_{-P}^{P}(P-|x|)\,dx &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times 2P\times P \\ &= P^2 \end{aligned}$$
So $P^2=16$, and with $P>0$:
$$P=4$$
The answer is option A.

parts.latex: What is the value of $\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{3}|x-1|\,dx$?

solutions.latex:
The expression $|x-1|$ equals $1-x$ for $x<1$ and $x-1$ for $x\ge1$, so split the integral at $x=1$:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_{-2}^{3}|x-1|\,dx &= \int_{-2}^{1}(1-x)\,dx+\int_{1}^{3}(x-1)\,dx \\ &= \left[x-\dfrac{x^2}{2}\right]_{-2}^{1}+\left[\dfrac{x^2}{2}-x\right]_{1}^{3} \\ &= \left(\dfrac{1}{2}-(-4)\right)+\left(\dfrac{3}{2}-\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\right) \\ &= \dfrac{9}{2}+2 \\ &= \dfrac{13}{2}\end{aligned}$$
Hence the answer is option D.

solutions.latex:
The denominator is zero when $3-3^x=0$, that is at $x=1$.

This lies inside $0\le x\le 4$, so there is a vertical asymptote there and the function is not continuous on the interval.

$$\therefore\ \text{the integral is meaningless}$$

parts.latex: Find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_0^8 \sqrt{64-x^2}\;dx$

$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^8\sqrt{64-x^2}\,dx&=\dfrac{\pi\times 8^2}{4}\\ &=16\pi\text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$
Hence the answer is option D.

parts.latex: What is the value of $\displaystyle\int_{-3}^{2}|x+1|\,dx$ ?

solutions.latex:
The integral of $|x+1|$ equals the area between the curve and the $x$-axis, which is two triangles meeting at $x=-1$.

On $[-3,-1]$ the triangle has base $2$ and height $2$. On $[-1,2]$ it has base $3$ and height $3$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_{-3}^{2}|x+1|\,dx&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times2\times2+\dfrac{1}{2}\times3\times3 \\ &=2+\dfrac{9}{2} \\ &=\dfrac{13}{2} \end{aligned}$$
Hence the answer is option C.

$$\begin{aligned} x^2-4x+y^2 &= 0 \\ (x^2-4x+4)+y^2 &= 4 &&(\text{add } 4 \text{ to both sides}) \\ (x-2)^2+y^2 &= 2^2 \end{aligned}$$

For $0\le x\le 2$ the region between the curve and the $x$-axis is the quarter of the circle above the $x$-axis and to the left of its centre $(2,0)$.
